**Audience**: an engineer who has already scraped a CSV of reviews / tickets and fitted a scikit-learn classifier — and wants to know *why* BM25 beats TF-IDF, or why a BERT fine-tune blows up the vocab. **Empirical first**: F1 dropping after aggressive stemming; a tokenizer that multiplies FR tokens vs EN — then we name BoW, embeddings, transformers.

From tokenization to industrial text mining (TF-IDF/BM25, embeddings, topics, NER, fine-tuning). Mandatory P2 foundation for the M2 module [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Build a complete text processing pipeline, from raw corpus to usable features.
-   Represent documents with bag of words, TF-IDF and BM25, build a search engine on these foundations (inverted index) and evaluate its rankings (MAP, nDCG).
-   Train and interpret word embeddings.
-   Infer latent topics in a corpus with topic models.
-   Classify texts, from Naive Bayes to transformer fine-tuning.
-   Label sequences (named entity recognition) with HMMs and CRFs, and extract relations between entities as knowledge-graph triples.
-   Fine-tune a transformer for a given NLP task, and assemble a minimal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline.
-   Build content-based and collaborative recommenders (matrix factorization), and use text features for click prediction and social media monitoring.
-   Conduct a text mining project in an industrial context, from data to production deployment.

### Course outline

-   **Review: vector spaces and probabilities** — the two lenses of the course: representing a document as a vector, reasoning in terms of laws and likelihood.
-   **The text processing pipeline** — segmentation, cleaning, normalization, subword tokenization and the first language model (n-grams with Kneser–Ney smoothing): the decisive craft before any model.
-   **Bag of words, TF-IDF and BM25** — the classical representations, the scoring function that powers information retrieval, the inverted index and ranking metrics.
-   **Text classification** — from Naive Bayes to neural models: the reference task of NLP.
-   **Word embeddings** — moving from counting to prediction: word vectors that carry meaning.
-   **Topic models** — discovering the latent topics of a corpus, with EM as the engine.
-   **Sequences and relations: NER, HMM, CRF, relation extraction** — labeling named entities with structured sequential models, training them, and linking entities into knowledge-graph triples.
-   **Transformers for NLP** — the transformer block, pretrained families, fine-tuning, sentence embeddings, and a minimal RAG pipeline.
-   **Industrial text mining** — summaries, keywords, deduplication, a ticket case study, recommendation systems, web advertising and social media analysis; volumes, annotation budgets, deployment and monitoring.
-   **Research at DaSciM (Vazirgiannis, Buscaldi)** — a tour of the research work of Vazirgiannis and Buscaldi (self-study).
-   **Exercises**, **Projects and assessment** and **References** — systematic training, project subjects with an exam and a rubric (proposals), and sources to go further.

### How to study this module

-   Work through the review section: dot products and conditional probabilities are used explicitly in every subsequent chapter.
-   Once, build a bag of words and a TF-IDF score yourself on a mini-corpus: everything that follows is understood by contrast with this baseline.
-   Before each model, write down on paper what it assumes (independence, word order, latency): this is what enables practical choices.
-   Hand-label a few sentences for a NER task: you will measure the cost of annotation, the central constraint of industrial NLP.
-   Read section 7.1 alongside the attention chapter of [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch6) (ch. 6) or the transformer-block section of [Deep Learning (P2)](../m1p2-deep-learning-p2/index.html#ch0) (ch. 0): the two reinforce each other.
-   Redo the exercises of each section before moving on to the next; they prepare the graded assignments and the bridge to the LLMs module.

## 0. Review: vector spaces and probabilities {#ch0}

This course reads text through two lenses: as vectors (a document is a point, similarity is an angle) and as random sequences (a document is drawn from a distribution, and learning means maximizing a likelihood). The review below recalls the tools of both lenses and points to the chapter where each one is used.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
L3 background used
:::

-   **Vector spaces**: basis, dimension, projection; cosine similarity
    $$
    \cos(u, v) = \frac{u^\top v}{\|u\|\,\|v\|}
    $$
    — invariant under dilation ($\cos(u,v)=\cos(\lambda u, v)$ for $\lambda > 0$, which "cancels out" document lengths); the $\ell_2$ norm will be used to normalize TF-IDF vectors;
-   **Linear algebra**: singular value decomposition
    $$
    \mathbf{X} \approx \mathbf{U}_k \Sigma_k \mathbf{V}_k^\top
    $$
    — the engine of LSA (ch. 5) and the direct cousin of PCA (Machine Learning module);
-   **Conditional probabilities and Bayes**:
    $$
    \mathbb{P}(c \mid d) \propto \mathbb{P}(d \mid c)\,\mathbb{P}(c)
    $$
    — the Naive Bayes classifier (ch. 3) follows directly from it; the Dirichlet distribution $\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha)$, conjugate of the multinomial — the foundation of LDA (ch. 5);
-   **Markov chains** ([Refresher Statistics](../m1p1-refresher-statistics/index.html#ch2) ch. 2, [Reinforcement Learning](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html#ch0) ch. 0) **and dynamic programming** ([Refresher CS](../m1p1-refresher-cs/index.html) 6.6): forward/backward and Viterbi (ch. 6) are Bellman recursions on a chain; TextRank (ch. 8) is a Markov chain raised to a power;
-   **Likelihood, MLE and EM**: word2vec (ch. 4), LDA (ch. 5), Naive Bayes (ch. 3) and the Unigram tokenizer (ch. 1) are all likelihood maximizations — by SGD, Gibbs, direct counting or EM;
-   **Entropy and perplexity**: for a language model,
    $$
    \mathrm{PPL} = \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{t} \log p(x_t \mid x_{<t})\big)
    $$
    — the universal quality measure of a generative model of text (M2 LLMs, ch. 3).
::::

::: note
[How to read this course]{.tag} Each chapter follows the same triptych:

1.  a *representation* of text (counts, weights, vectors, distributions, latent topics);
2.  a learning *algorithm* with its statistical justification;
3.  a quantified *evaluation*.

The [thm]{.tag}/prop boxes contain the proven results; the proofs come at the end of each box. References of the form "module X, chapter N" point to the other courses of the master's program.

The natural extension of this module is the M2 "Large Language Models" course, which picks up tokenization (ch. 1), BM25 (ch. 2), sentence embeddings (ch. 7) and transformers where we leave them.
:::

## 1. The text processing pipeline {#ch1}

Concrete scene: 50,000 support tickets in French and English. A first pipeline lowercases the text, splits it into "words" with a regular expression and feeds TF-IDF features to a logistic regression: macro-F1 0.62. Without NFKC normalization, two encodings of "café" count as two different types; with aggressive stemming, "connection" and "connector" merge and the macro-F1 drops to 0.51. This chapter fixes the pipeline *before* the model.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Inconsistent train/prod tokenizer (ghost vocab); normalizing too late (Unicode duplicates); judging a classifier on overall accuracy when 3 classes dominate. All three sabotage an LLM fine-tune as much as a toy BoW.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Standard pipeline]{.tag} **Raw text** → cleaning (HTML, case, accents, Unicode) → sentence segmentation → **tokenization** (splitting into units: words, subwords, characters) → lexical normalization (*stemming* raw root / *lemmatization* canonical form; stopwords) → representation (ch. 2, 4, 5) → model (ch. 3, 6, 7) → evaluation. Each stage destroys information; the engineer's craft is deciding *which* information is expendable for the task at hand.
:::

### 1.1. Unicode normalization and "clean" text

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Unicode normal forms]{.tag} The same glyph admits several encodings: "é" = one codepoint `U+00E9` in **NFC** (canonical composition), but two (`e` + combining accent `U+0301`) in **NFD**. **NFKC** goes further: ligature "ﬁ" → "fi", digit "²" → "2", full-width letters → ASCII. Two strings that are visually identical but distinct in bytes break counting, deduplication and search; so we normalize *before anything else* (in practice NFKC, or NFC if typography and units must be preserved).
:::

-   **Case**: `lower()` merges "Polytechnique" and "polytechnique" but also the acronym and the common word; in French, *keep the accents* in lowercase ("élève" ≠ "eleve");
-   **Sentence segmentation**: rules (punctuation + capital letter) or learning (Punkt, Kiss & Strunk 2006); real pitfalls: "M.", "etc.", German abbreviations ("z. B."), period before a closing quote. Bad segmentation wrecks ch. 8 (extractive summarization: the sentence is the unit being selected);
-   **Stemming vs lemmatization**: the stemmer (Porter, Snowball) cuts off suffixes by rules — fast, crude, suited to information retrieval; the lemmatizer uses a dictionary and morphology ("sont" → "être") — slower, better for fine-grained analysis. In industry: stemmer for search, lemmatizer for analysis.

### 1.2. Subword tokenization: BPE, WordPiece, Unigram, SentencePiece

::: note
[Why subwords]{.tag} Splitting on spaces works poorly: German compounds ("Donaudampfschifffahrt"), French elisions ("l'arbre": 1 or 2 tokens?), some Asian languages write without spaces, and any closed vocabulary runs into unknown words (typos, neologisms, product references). **Subword tokenizers** learn, on the corpus, a fixed-size vocabulary (\~32k-128k) whose concatenation reconstructs *any* string: frequent words = 1 token, rare words = a sequence of pieces.
:::

::: thm
[Algorithm 1.3 — BPE (Byte Pair Encoding, Sennrich et al. 2016)]{.tag} Initial vocabulary: characters (or bytes). Iteratively: (1) count all pairs of adjacent symbols in the corpus (weighted by word frequencies); (2) merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol; (3) repeat until the vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$ reaches the target size $|\mathcal{V}|$. The result is an ordered set of *merge rules*; tokenizing a new text = applying the merges in the learned order.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.4 — Step-by-step BPE training]{.tag} Mini-corpus (words, frequencies): `base`×5, `bases`×4, `basse`×3, `basique`×2. Initial alphabet: b, a, s, e, i, q, u. We write each word as a sequence of symbols and count adjacent pairs:

  Step   Most frequent pairs                                                         Chosen merge
  ------ --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------------------
  1      (b,a)=14, (a,s)=14, (s,e)=12, (e,s)=4, (s,s)=3, (s,i)=(i,q)=(q,u)=(u,e)=2   **ba** (14; tie with (a,s), arbitrary choice)
  2      (ba,s)=14, (s,e)=12, (e,s)=4, (s,s)=3, …                                    **bas** (14)
  3      (bas,e)=9, (e,s)=4, (bas,s)=3, (s,e)=3, …                                   **base** (9)
  4      (base,s)=4, (bas,s)=3, (s,e)=3, …                                           **bases** (4)
  5      (bas,s)=3, (s,e)=3, …                                                       **bass** (3)
  6      (bass,e)=3, …                                                               **basse** (3)

After these six merges, `base`, `bases` and `basse` are whole tokens, while `basique` is still `bas`+`i`+`q`+`u`+`e` (four more merges would make it whole); an unexpected word like "basiste" breaks down into a known prefix (`bas`, or `basi` once more merges are learned) followed by single characters: never an unknown token, at worst a longer sequence. *This is exactly the mechanism that equips GPT (byte-level BPE since GPT-2, 50k tokens; about 100k for GPT-4) and Llama 3 (byte-level BPE, 128k tokens) — developed in M2 LLMs, ch. 1.*
:::

::: thm
[Variants 1.5 — WordPiece (BERT), Unigram (T5), SentencePiece]{.tag}

-   **WordPiece**: the same merge loop, but a pair's score is $\frac{f(x,y)}{f(x)\,f(y)}$ — we merge the pair whose *relative* frequency increases the most, a proxy for the likelihood gain of a unigram model (justification: merging $x,y$ replaces two symbols with one; the gain in bits is all the greater as the collocation is over-represented relative to independence);
-   **Unigram** (Kudo, 2018): a *generative* model — a candidate vocabulary (characters + frequent substrings), each segment $s$ has a probability $p(s)$, a word is segmented by Viterbi by maximizing $\sum_j \log p(s_j)$.

    Training by EM: **E** — for each word, the posterior distribution over its segmentations (∝ product of the $p(s_j)$, computable by a forward dynamic program); **M** — $p(s)$ = normalized expected counts; then *pruning* of the segments that degrade the likelihood the least, until the target size $|\mathcal{V}|$.

    Unlike BPE, the segmentation is probabilistic and admits several analyses (subword regularization);
-   **SentencePiece**: a *language-independent* layer that treats the sentence as a sequence of bytes, the space becoming a "▁" symbol; no pre-tokenization on spaces — essential for languages without spaces and for multilingual settings. It is the tokenizer of T5 (a Unigram model) and of Llama 1 and 2 (a 32k BPE model); Llama 3 moved to the 128k byte-level BPE of Example 1.4.
:::

```python
import re
from collections import Counter

# --- Toy BPE: learning merges on the mini-corpus of example 1.4 ---
words = {"b a s e": 5, "b a s e s": 4, "b a s s e": 3, "b a s i q u e": 2}
merges = []
for _ in range(8):
    pairs = Counter()
    for w, f in words.items():
        sym = w.split()
        for pair in zip(sym, sym[1:]):
            pairs[pair] += f
    if not pairs:
        break
    best = max(pairs, key=pairs.get)          # most frequent adjacent pair
    merges.append(best)
    big = " ".join(best)
    words = {re.sub(r"(?<!\S)" + re.escape(big) + r"(?!\S)", "".join(best), w): f
             for w, f in words.items()}
print("merges:", merges[:6])
# tokenize a new word = replay the merges in the learned order
def encode(word, merges):
    sym = list(word)
    for a, b in merges:
        i, out = 0, []
        while i < len(sym):
            if i + 1 < len(sym) and (sym[i], sym[i+1]) == (a, b):
                out.append(a + b); i += 2
            else:
                out.append(sym[i]); i += 1
        sym = out
    return sym
print(encode("basiste", merges))
```

### 1.3. Stopwords, n-grams, collocations and n-gram language models {#ngram-lm}

-   **Stopwords**: to be removed for classical text mining (they saturate the BoW); to be *kept* for transformers — negation ("ne…pas") and syntax matter. The decision must be justified by the task, not by habit;
-   **N-grams**: sequences of $n$ tokens; "New York" (bigram) ≠ "New" + "York"; in classification, moving from unigrams to bigrams captures compositional polarity ("pas cher"); cost: the vocabulary explodes (potentially $|\mathcal{V}|^n$) — hence `ngram_range=(1,2)` and `min_df` in the code of ch. 3;
-   **Collocations**: bigrams whose frequency exceeds what independence predicts, measured by mutual information $\mathrm{PMI}(x,y) = \log \frac{P(x,y)}{P(x)P(y)}$ — a criterion reused as-is in ch. 2 to justify IDF, and in ch. 5 for topic coherence.

Counting n-grams also gives the first *language model*: a probability for the next word given the previous ones. It is the ancestor of the LLMs of M2, it is still the language model of classical speech recognizers ([Speech Technology](../m2-speech-technology/index.html#ch1), ch. 1), and its central difficulty — how much probability to leave for what was never seen — never goes away.

:::: thm
[Model 1.6 — Bigram language model with interpolated Kneser–Ney smoothing]{.tag} A bigram model factorizes a sentence as
$$
p(w_{1:N})=\prod_{t} p(w_t\mid w_{t-1}).
$$
The maximum-likelihood estimate $c(v,w)/c(v)$ gives probability zero to every bigram absent from the training corpus, so a single unseen bigram makes a whole test sentence impossible.

Interpolated Kneser–Ney (Kneser & Ney, 1995; Chen & Goodman, 1999) subtracts a fixed discount $D \in (0, 1]$, typically $0.75$, from every seen count and gives the freed mass to a *continuation* distribution:

::: key
[Key result — interpolated Kneser–Ney bigram]{.tag}
$$
p_{\mathrm{KN}}(w\mid v)=\frac{\max\big(c(v,w)-D,\,0\big)}{c(v)}+\lambda(v)\,p_{\mathrm{cont}}(w),
\qquad
\lambda(v)=\frac{D\,N_{1+}(v\,\bullet)}{c(v)},
\qquad
p_{\mathrm{cont}}(w)=\frac{N_{1+}(\bullet\,w)}{N_{1+}(\bullet\,\bullet)}
$$
:::

Here $N_{1+}(v\,\bullet)$ is the number of distinct words seen after $v$, $N_{1+}(\bullet\,w)$ the number of distinct words seen before $w$, and $N_{1+}(\bullet\,\bullet)$ the number of distinct bigram types.

Reading: the continuation probability asks "in how many contexts does $w$ appear?", not "how often?". "Francisco" is frequent but appears almost only after "San", so it receives little continuation mass and is not predicted after unrelated words.

::: proof
The model is a distribution. Let $c(v)$ count the occurrences of $v$ followed by a word. Every seen bigram has $c(v,w)\ge 1\ge D$, so
$$
\sum_w \frac{\max\big(c(v,w)-D,\,0\big)}{c(v)}=\frac{c(v)-D\,N_{1+}(v\,\bullet)}{c(v)}=1-\lambda(v),
$$
and the second term adds $\lambda(v)\sum_w p_{\mathrm{cont}}(w)=\lambda(v)$. The total is $1$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

*Example* — counts from a training corpus:

-   "the" is followed by a word 10 times, by 4 distinct words, 3 times by "cat" and never by "dog";
-   the corpus has 200 bigram types; "cat" follows 5 distinct words and "dog" follows 20;
-   with $D=0.75$, the back-off weight is $\lambda(\text{the})=0.75\cdot 4/10=0.3$.

Then
$$
p_{\mathrm{KN}}(\text{cat}\mid\text{the})=\frac{2.25}{10}+0.3\cdot\frac{5}{200}=0.2325,
\qquad
p_{\mathrm{KN}}(\text{dog}\mid\text{the})=0+0.3\cdot\frac{20}{200}=0.03 .
$$
::::

::: def
[Definition 1.7 — Perplexity]{.tag} On a held-out text of $N$ tokens,
$$
\mathrm{PPL}=\exp\Big(-\frac1N\sum_{t=1}^{N}\log p(w_t\mid w_{<t})\Big),
$$
the exponential of the average negative log-likelihood (the cross-entropy, in nats).

It reads as an *effective branching factor*: a model that is uniform over $\mathcal{V}$ has perplexity $|\mathcal{V}|$, and a model with perplexity 50 is as uncertain, on average, as a uniform choice among 50 words. Lower is better. Two perplexities are comparable only with the same tokenizer and the same test text: a subword model and a word model do not count the same $N$.

*Example*: four test tokens predicted with probabilities 0.25, 0.5, 0.1 and 0.2 have a mean log-probability of $-1.498$, so
$$
\mathrm{PPL}=e^{1.498}\approx 4.47 .
$$
:::

## 2. Bag of words, TF-IDF and BM25 {#ch2}

Most models cannot read strings: they need vectors. This chapter turns each document into a vector of word counts, reweights the counts so that informative words dominate (TF-IDF), and derives BM25, the scoring function that still powers search engines.

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Bag of words (BoW)]{.tag} A document = a vector of counts over the vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$ (order lost): $d \in \mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{V}|}$. Documents × terms matrix $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{N}^{n \times |\mathcal{V}|}$ — *extremely sparse* (a few hundred non-zeros per document across tens of thousands of columns; sparse representation, cf. Refresher CS).
:::

::::: def
[Definition 2.2 — TF-IDF]{.tag}

::: key
[Key result — TF-IDF weight]{.tag}
$$
\mathrm{tfidf}(t, d) = \mathrm{tf}(t, d) \times \underbrace{\log\frac{n}{\mathrm{df}(t)}}_{\mathrm{idf}(t)},
$$
:::

$\mathrm{tf}$ = frequency of the term in the document, $\mathrm{df}$ = number of documents containing the term, $n$ = number of documents. It penalizes omnipresent terms and rewards discriminative ones.

**L2 weighting**: we post-normalize $\tilde d = d / \|d\|_2$, so that *the dot product is directly the cosine similarity* — this is what `TfidfVectorizer` does by default.
:::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.3 — IDF = pointwise mutual information]{.tag} Let us choose a document $D$ uniformly among the $n$, and let $T$ denote the event "$D$ contains the term $t$".

Then for any document $d$ containing $t$:
$$
\mathrm{PMI}(T\,;D=d) \;=\; \log\frac{\mathbb{P}(T,\,D=d)}{\mathbb{P}(T)\,\mathbb{P}(D=d)} \;=\; \log\frac{n}{\mathrm{df}(t)} \;=\; \mathrm{idf}(t).
$$

In other words: IDF is exactly the pointwise mutual information between "the event $t$ occurs" and the choice of this particular document. A term present everywhere identifies no document (zero PMI); a rare term strongly identifies the documents that contain it.

::: proof
$\mathbb{P}(D=d)=1/n$ and $\mathbb{P}(T)=\mathrm{df}(t)/n$, so $\mathbb{P}(T,D=d)=\frac{1}{n}\,\mathbf{1}[t\in d]$. Substituting:
$$
\mathrm{PMI} = \log\frac{\mathbf{1}[t\in d]/n}{(\mathrm{df}/n)(1/n)} = \log\frac{n\,\mathbf{1}[t\in d]}{\mathrm{df}},
$$
which equals $\mathrm{idf}(t)$ if $t \in d$ (and $-\infty$ otherwise). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Common variants (all useful in practice)]{.tag}

-   **Sublinear TF**: $1+\log \mathrm{tf}$ — "3 occurrences do not signal the topic 3× more than a single one";
-   **Boolean TF**: $\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{tf}>0]$ — robust to highly repetitive documents (spam, bots);
-   **Smoothed IDF**: $\log\frac{1+n}{1+\mathrm{df}}+1$ (the scikit-learn variant) — avoids blow-ups for $\mathrm{df}=n$;
-   **Composite schemes** (SMART nomenclature): different weighting on the document side (e.g. L2 of log-tf × idf) and on the query side (e.g. plain cosine); the performance of a search engine is often tuned here, before any model.
:::

:::: thm
[Model 2.4 — BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza) and its probabilistic reading]{.tag} A direct heir of probabilistic information retrieval (the Robertson–Sparck Jones 2-Poisson framework): a document is a mixture of "informative / non-informative" for the query.

The number of occurrences $x$ of the term follows a Poisson law of intensity $\mu_1$ in the documents that are really *about* the term ("elite" documents) and of intensity $\mu_0 \ll \mu_1$ in the others, and relevance is only correlated with eliteness.

The resulting weight of $x$ is the log-odds of relevance under this *mixture*: it is $0$ at $x = 0$, increasing, and *saturating* as $x$ grows (for a single pair of Poisson laws, the log-likelihood ratio $\;x\log\frac{\mu_1}{\mu_0}-(\mu_1-\mu_0)\;$ would grow linearly; it is the mixture that bounds it).

BM25 approximates this shape:

::: key
[Key result — the BM25 score]{.tag}
$$
\mathrm{BM25}(q,d)=\sum_{t\in q}\mathrm{idf}_{25}(t)\cdot \frac{\mathrm{tf}(t,d)\,(k_1+1)}{\mathrm{tf}(t,d)+k_1\!\left(1-b+b\,\frac{|d|}{\mathrm{avgdl}}\right)},\qquad \mathrm{idf}_{25}(t)=\log\frac{n-\mathrm{df}(t)+0.5}{\mathrm{df}(t)+0.5},
$$
:::

where $|d|$ is the length of $d$ in tokens, $\mathrm{avgdl}$ the average length over the corpus, and $k_1 \in [1.2, 2]$, $b = 0.75$ the usual defaults of the two tuning parameters.

::: proof
Two limits to know by heart.

-   **Saturation**: as $\mathrm{tf}\to\infty$, the factor tends to $k_1+1$ (bounded); at $\mathrm{tf}=0$ it equals $0$.
-   **Half-saturation**: it reaches half of its maximum when
    $$
    \mathrm{tf}=k_1(1-b+b|d|/\mathrm{avgdl})
    $$
    — $k_1$ tunes the saturation speed, $b$ the length penalty ($b=0$: no normalization; $b=1$: proportional).

These are exactly the two flaws of raw TF-IDF that BM25 corrects: unbounded linear growth on the tf side, and no handling of document length. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

|  | TF-IDF + cosine | BM25 | Set similarities | WMD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Formula | $\mathrm{tf}\cdot\mathrm{idf}$, normalized dot product | probabilistic weighting, saturating tf | Jaccard $\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|}$ | transport distance between embeddings |
| What matters | weighted presence | presence *and* saturated density | set overlap | semantic alignment of words |
| Typical use | classification features (ch. 3) | search / retrieval (ch. 8, M2 ch. 7) | fast deduplication (ch. 8) | fine-grained similarity of short sentences |
| Cost | linear, sparse | linear, sparse | linear | linear program (Optimal Transport module) |

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.5 — Hashing trick for giant vocabularies]{.tag} For huge or *a priori unbounded* $|\mathcal{V}|$ (tweet streams, logs): hash each term $h(t) \in \{1,\dots,D\}$ with a random sign $s(t)\in\{\pm1\}$, and set $\tilde x_i = \sum_{t:\,h(t)=i} s(t)\,x_t$. Then
$$
\mathbb{E}\,\langle \tilde x,\tilde y\rangle = \langle x,y\rangle
$$
— collisions cancel out *in expectation*.

::: proof
We have
$$
\tilde x^\top\tilde y = \sum_{t,t'} s(t)s(t')\,x_t y_{t'}\,\mathbf{1}[h(t)=h(t')]
$$
and $\mathbb{E}[s(t)s(t')]=\mathbf{1}[t=t']$ (independent signs); what remains is $\sum_t x_t y_t$.

The standard deviation of the collision term decreases like $1/\sqrt{D}$: with $D\sim 2^{20}$, the approximation is excellent for classification. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Geometry of documents]{.tag} Each document becomes a point in $\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}$; we measure similarities (cosine), classify (Naive Bayes, SVM), cluster (k-means). The limitation of BoW: *bag* = no order and no semantics; "the cat eats the mouse" ≈ "the mouse eats the cat".

Embeddings (ch. 4) and transformers (ch. 7) answer this. BM25 remains *the* baseline of any retrieval system — including RAG (M2 LLMs, ch. 7, where it serves as a reference point for dense retrievers).
:::

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi

corpus = ["graphe de connaissances entreprise",
          "réseau de neurones profond",
          "graphe neuronal et réseau d'entreprise"]
X = TfidfVectorizer().fit_transform(corpus)      # sparse matrix (3, vocabulary size), L2-normalized
print(cosine_similarity(X).round(2))             # docs 0 and 2 are the closest

toks = [d.split() for d in corpus]
bm25 = BM25Okapi(toks)
print(bm25.get_scores("réseau entreprise".split()))  # BM25 score per document
```

### 2.1. Search engines: inverted index and ranking evaluation

Information retrieval, named first among the applications of the official description, needs two more ingredients than a scoring function: a data structure that avoids scoring every document, and a way to measure whether the ranking is good.

::: def
[Definition 2.6 — Inverted index]{.tag} For each term $t$, the index stores a *posting list* of pairs $(\text{doc id}, \mathrm{tf}(t, d))$ sorted by document id, together with $\mathrm{df}(t)$ and the document lengths $|d|$.

A query $q$ reads only the posting lists of its own terms, at cost $\sum_{t \in q} \mathrm{df}(t)$ instead of $n\,|q|$; scores (TF-IDF, BM25) are accumulated per document and the top $k$ kept in a heap.

Because the BM25 term factor is bounded by $k_1 + 1$ (Model 2.4), each term has an upper bound on its contribution, and *dynamic pruning* (MaxScore, WAND) skips documents that cannot enter the current top $k$.

Posting lists store the *gaps* between consecutive ids with variable-length codes; by Zipf's law most terms are rare, so most lists are short.
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.7 — Ranking evaluation]{.tag} For a query with $R$ relevant documents and a ranked list:

-   **Precision@k** $= \#\{\text{relevant in the top } k\}/k$;
-   **Recall@k** $= \#\{\text{relevant in the top } k\}/R$;
-   **average precision**
    $$
    \mathrm{AP} = \frac{1}{R}\sum_{k\,:\,\text{doc at rank } k \text{ relevant}} \mathrm{P@}k,
    $$
    and MAP its mean over queries;
-   **reciprocal rank** $1/\text{rank of the first relevant document}$ (MRR over queries).

With graded relevance $\mathrm{rel}_i$:
$$
\mathrm{DCG@}k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{2^{\mathrm{rel}_i} - 1}{\log_2(i + 1)}, \qquad \mathrm{nDCG@}k = \frac{\mathrm{DCG@}k}{\mathrm{IDCG@}k} \in [0, 1],
$$
where IDCG is the DCG of the ideal ordering. These are also the metrics of the retrievers of RAG systems (M2 LLMs, ch. 7) and of the recommenders of section 8.5.
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.8 — Evaluating one ranked list]{.tag} A collection has $R = 3$ relevant documents for a query, and the engine returns five documents judged (relevant, not, relevant, not, relevant).

-   Precision: $\mathrm{P@}1 = 1$, $\mathrm{P@}3 = 2/3$, $\mathrm{P@}5 = 3/5$.
-   Average precision:
    $$
    \mathrm{AP} = \frac13\big(1 + \frac23 + \frac35\big) \approx 0.756 ;
    $$
    the reciprocal rank is $1$.
-   With graded judgments $(3, 0, 2, 0, 1)$:
    $$
    \mathrm{DCG@}5 = \frac{7}{1} + \frac{3}{\log_2 4} + \frac{1}{\log_2 6} \approx 7 + 1.5 + 0.387 = 8.887 ;
    $$
-   the ideal order $(3, 2, 1, 0, 0)$ gives
    $$
    \mathrm{IDCG@}5 = 7 + \frac{3}{\log_2 3} + \frac{1}{2} \approx 9.393 .
    $$

So $\mathrm{nDCG@}5 \approx 0.946$.

Swapping the documents at ranks 2 and 3 gives $(3, 2, 0, 0, 1)$ and $\mathrm{nDCG@}5 \approx 9.280/9.393 \approx 0.988$, the best single swap but not yet the ideal list: the grade-1 document at rank 5 must also move up to rank 3, which takes a second swap.
:::

## 3. Text classification {#ch3}

Deciding which category a document belongs to — spam or not, which team should handle a ticket, positive or negative review — is the most common NLP task in industry. This chapter builds the two reference classifiers on the bag-of-words vectors of ch. 2, Naive Bayes and regularized logistic regression, together with the evaluation practice that goes with them.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.1 — Multinomial Naive Bayes, derived]{.tag} With the (false!) assumption of word independence given the class,
$$
\mathbb{P}(d\mid c)=\prod_{t\in d}\mathbb{P}(t\mid c)^{\mathrm{tf}(t,d)},
$$
and Bayes:
$$
\hat c = \arg\max_c \Big[\log \mathbb{P}(c) + \sum_{t\in d}\mathrm{tf}(t,d)\log \mathbb{P}(t\mid c)\Big].
$$

MLE of the parameters:
$$
\mathbb{P}(t\mid c)=\frac{n_{t,c}}{n_c},
$$
where $n_{t,c}$ is the number of occurrences of $t$ in the documents of class $c$ and $n_c = \sum_t n_{t,c}$, and
$$
\mathbb{P}(c)=\frac{N_c}{N}
$$
($N_c$ documents of class $c$ among $N$).

**Laplace smoothing**:
$$
\mathbb{P}(t\mid c)=\frac{n_{t,c}+1}{n_c+|\mathcal{V}|}.
$$

::: proof
1.  The MLE comes from maximizing the multinomial log-likelihood under the constraint $\sum_t \mathbb{P}(t\mid c)=1$ (Lagrange multipliers — relative counts).
2.  Problem: a word seen at test time but never in class $c$ gives $\log 0 = -\infty$ — a single rare word wipes out the whole class, and on small corpora this happens constantly.
3.  Laplace smoothing is the *posterior mean* under a uniform Dirichlet$(1,\dots,1)$ prior: the posterior density
    $$
    \propto \prod_t \pi_t^{n_{t,c}}\cdot\prod_t\pi_t^{1-1}
    $$
    is that of a Dirichlet$(n_{1,c}+1, \dots, n_{|\mathcal{V}|,c}+1)$, whose mean is $\frac{n_{t,c}+1}{n_c+|\mathcal{V}|}$ (equivalently, it is the MAP under a Dirichlet$(2,\dots,2)$ prior) — the exact Bayesian link of ch. 0. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Why NB works despite an absurd assumption]{.tag} Conditional independence is massively violated ("New" predicts "York"). But the *decision* (argmax) is often correct even when the *probabilities* are badly calibrated: it is enough for the right candidate to win, not for its score to be right (the theory of Domingos & Pazzani). Hence NB's status: bad probabilities, good baseline — always the *first* one in a text project, because it trains in seconds and sets the performance floor.
:::

::: prop
[Sparse logistic regression: why it works in high dimension]{.tag} On TF-IDF, $\#\text{features} \gg \#\text{docs}$ (10⁵ features for 10³ documents): the risk of overfitting seems maximal, yet the regularized linear model (L2, or L1 to select) generalizes very well. Three reasons:

1.  in high dimension the vectors are *almost orthogonal* — examples are naturally separable, and regularization suffices to pick a "sober" separator;
2.  IDF weighting has already done a large share of the statistical work (prop. 2.3);
3.  discriminative unigrams/bigrams are exactly the features a linear model weights well.

State of the art of the "classical" era until 2018 (Joulin et al., fastText); still formidable below 1,000 labeled examples.
:::

-   **Calibration**: when the probability is consumed (business thresholds, ticket routing), recalibrate — Platt (logistic regression on the scores) or isotonic; diagnostic: reliability curve (predicted vs observed reliability);
-   **Imbalanced classes**: class weighting (`class_weight="balanced"`), optimal threshold on the PR curve (not ROC); metric: **macro-F1** (per-class average — every class counts equally) rather than accuracy (which flatters the majority); per-intent confusion matrix for chatbots;
-   **Networks**: sentence CNNs (Kim, 2014) and BiLSTMs over the word embeddings of ch. 4; then transformer fine-tuning (ch. 7). Empirical learning curves: linear+TF-IDF wins below \~10²-10³ examples, the transformer above;
-   **Zero-shot / few-shot with an LLM**: zero labeled examples, or $k$ examples in the prompt; the mechanism is stated in the box of section 7.2 and studied in depth in [M2 LLMs](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch4) (ch. 4.0, prompting and in-context learning). An excellent exploratory starting point and a help for labeling (active learning), rarely the final solution in production (cost, latency, confidentiality).

```python
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_20newsgroups
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, classification_report

train = fetch_20newsgroups(subset="train", remove=("headers","footers","quotes"))
test  = fetch_20newsgroups(subset="test",  remove=("headers","footers","quotes"))

pipe = make_pipeline(TfidfVectorizer(min_df=3, ngram_range=(1,2), sublinear_tf=True),
                     LogisticRegression(C=10, max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced"))
pipe.fit(train.data, train.target)
pred = pipe.predict(test.data)
print("macro-F1:", f1_score(test.target, pred, average="macro"))
print(classification_report(test.target, pred, labels=[0, 1, 2],   # first 3 of the 20 classes
                            target_names=test.target_names[:3]))
```

## 4. Word embeddings {#ch4}

In a bag of words, "car" and "automobile" are as different as "car" and "banana": every word is its own orthogonal axis. Word embeddings replace these axes by dense vectors of a few hundred dimensions, learned from the contexts in which words appear, so that words used in similar contexts get similar vectors.

::: thm
[word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013): distributional hypothesis]{.tag} "A word is characterized by the company it keeps" (Firth, 1957). Each word has two vectors: a *center* vector $v_w$, used when $w$ sits at the current position, and a *context* vector $u_c$, used when it appears in the window of another word.

**Skip-gram**: for each position $t$ with center word $w_t$, maximize the log-likelihood of the context words $c$ within a window,
$$
\sum_{t}\sum_{c\in \mathrm{window}(t)} \log p(c\mid w_t), \qquad p(c\mid w)=\frac{\exp(u_c^\top v_w)}{\sum_{c'\in \mathcal{V}}\exp(u_{c'}^\top v_w)}
$$
— a softmax over the $|\mathcal{V}|$ words of the vocabulary at each position: $\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}|)$ per example, prohibitive. **CBOW**: symmetric (predict the word from the average of its context).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 4.1 — Negative sampling: the derived loss]{.tag} For one observed pair (center $w$, context $c$), we draw $k$ "negatives"
$$
n_1,\dots,n_k \sim p_n,\qquad p_n(x)\propto \mathrm{freq}(x)^{3/4}
$$
(the unigram distribution raised to the power 3/4) and replace the softmax with $k+1$ binary classifications "is this (center, word) pair a true context pair?". The loss, to be *minimized*, is
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{neg}} = -\log\sigma(u_c^\top v_w) - \sum_{i=1}^{k}\log\sigma(-u_{n_i}^\top v_w),
$$
at a cost of $\mathcal{O}(k)$ instead of $\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}|)$. Averaged over the draws, the sum over negatives becomes
$$
k\,\mathbb{E}_{n\sim p_n}\big[\log\sigma(-u_n^\top v_w)\big].
$$

The gradient in $v_w$:
$$
\nabla_{v_w}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{neg}} = -\big(1-\sigma(u_c^\top v_w)\big)\,u_c \;+\; \sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma(u_{n_i}^\top v_w)\,u_{n_i}.
$$

Reading: a descent step moves $v_w$ *toward* the context vector $u_c$, with a force $1-\sigma$ that vanishes once the pair is well predicted, and *away* from each negative, with a force equal to its current score $\sigma$ — a negative that the model wrongly scores high (often a semantically close word!) receives the largest correction.

After training, the center vectors are kept as the word embeddings. The rest of the chapter writes $z_w$ for the embedding of $w$ whatever the method (here $z_w = v_w$).

Theoretical interpretation: negative sampling is a form of NCE (noise contrastive estimation, Gutmann & Hyvärinen 2010; cf. Goldberg & Levy 2014).
:::

::: note
[Two settings that matter (and why)]{.tag}

-   **Frequency subsampling**: very frequent words ("the", "of") drown the signal; they are discarded with probability $p_{\mathrm{discard}}(w)=1-\sqrt{t/f(w)}$ (threshold $t\sim10^{-5}$ to $10^{-3}$) — the signal per pair stays intact and the computation is sped up;
-   **The 3/4 exponent**: flattening the frequencies boosts rare negatives, which are the most informative ones (frequent negatives are trivial to repel). The same exponent reappears in the weighting function of GloVe below: an empirical compromise between signal and coverage.
:::

::: thm
[GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014): least squares on cooccurrences]{.tag} Let $X_{ij}$ be the number of cooccurrences (words $i,j$) in the corpus. GloVe factorizes $\log X_{ij}$ with a *weighted* bilinear model:
$$
J=\sum_{i,j} f\!\left(X_{ij}\right)\big(z_i^\top \tilde z_j + b_i + \tilde b_j - \log X_{ij}\big)^2,\qquad f(x)=\min\!\Big[\big(x/x_{\max}\big)^{3/4},\,1\Big],
$$
where $f$ cuts the weight of rare cooccurrences (noisy, possibly zero; one cannot take $\log 0$) and saturates for frequent ones. The biases $b_i,\tilde b_j$ absorb the marginal frequencies.

Deep connection: skip-gram with negative sampling *is* an implicit factorization of a shifted PMI matrix (Levy & Goldberg, NeurIPS 2014). When the dot products are unconstrained, the optimum of the expected loss of Theorem 4.1 is
$$
u_c^\top v_w=\mathrm{PMI}(w,c)-\log k,
$$
where the PMI uses the noise distribution $p_n(c)$ in place of the context frequency $P(c)$. GloVe does it explicitly, and globally (the whole matrix at once) rather than locally (sampled windows).
:::

::: def
[fastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017): subwords]{.tag} A word = the sum of the vectors of its character $n$-grams (3 to 6): $z_w = \sum_{g\in G_w} z_g$. Consequences: an out-of-vocabulary word still receives a vector (the sum of its $n$-grams), and typos and rich morphology (German: compounds; French: conjugations) are absorbed. The same team shows that "fastText + bigrams" is a formidable classification baseline (cf. ch. 3).
:::

### 4.1. Evaluating embeddings

-   **Lexical similarity**: rate word pairs (SimLex-999, WordSim-353), correlate with the cosine — metric: Spearman correlation;
-   **Analogies**: precision@1 on $z_b - z_a + z_c \approx z_d$ excluding $\{a,b,c\}$ from the search (the Mikolov protocol): "king − man + woman ≈ queen". Caution: analogy accuracy is sensitive to word frequency;
-   **Downstream**: the real evaluation is the final task (ch. 3).

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — SIF sentence embeddings (Arora et al., TACL 2017)]{.tag} Sentence = weighted average with $a(w)=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+p(w)}$, where $p(w)$ is the relative frequency of $w$ in the corpus (an anti-frequency weight; $\alpha\sim10^{-3}$), *then* removal of the first principal component of the corpus:
$$
\bar v(S)=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{w\in S}\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+p(w)}\,z_w,\qquad v(S) = \bar v(S) - u_1 u_1^\top \bar v(S),
$$
with $|S|$ the number of words of $S$ and $u_1$ the first singular vector of the matrix whose rows are the $\bar v(S)$ of all the sentences of the corpus.

::: proof
Why remove $u_1$: in the generative model of Arora et al., each sentence is emitted around a "discourse vector" $c_S$, but a common vector $c_0$ (syntax, function words) biases *all* the sentences of the corpus — that is exactly the direction of greatest variance, hence $u_1$.

The orthogonal projection removes this shared nuisance term; on Semantic Textual Similarity (STS), this single removal gains several correlation points and makes this baseline "simple but hard to beat" without a trained encoder. It is the direct ancestor of SBERT embeddings (ch. 7). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[Bias in embeddings — the WEAT test (Caliskan et al., 2017)]{.tag} Two sets of target words $X,Y$ (e.g. professions) and two attributes $A,B$ (e.g. male/female first names). Association score
$$
s(w)=\frac{1}{|A|}\sum_{a\in A}\cos(z_w,z_a)-\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{b\in B}\cos(z_w,z_b);
$$
test statistic
$$
t = \frac{\mathrm{mean}_{x\in X}\,s(x)-\mathrm{mean}_{y\in Y}\,s(y)} {\mathrm{sd}_{w\in X\cup Y}\,s(w)},
$$
significance by permutations of the targets.

On GloVe/word2vec: scientific professions associate with the male attribute, artistic ones with the female — the corpus contains these stereotypes, and the geometry encodes them.

**Mitigation** (Bolukbasi et al., 2016): estimate the bias direction (PCA of the "he/she" pairs…), *neutralize* neutral words (remove their projection onto this direction) and *equalize* the pairs — we will see the "representation → bias → correction" pattern again in M2 (LLM safety, ch. 9 of the LLMs module).
:::

::: note
[Text ↔ graphs, the other LLGA bridge]{.tag} word2vec on *random walks* yields DeepWalk/node2vec (Graph ML module, ch. 3); conversely, a **Graph of Words** (nodes = words, edges = cooccurrence within a window) enables text mining with graph tools — this is a research axis of the course's professor, detailed in ch. 9: the words ↔ graphs loop is a signature of the master's program.
:::

```python
import gensim.downloader as api
wv = api.load("glove-wiki-gigaword-100")        # pretrained embeddings

def analogy(a, b, c):                            # a - b + c ≈ ?
    v = wv[a] - wv[b] + wv[c]
    return wv.most_similar(v, topn=3)
print(analogy("king", "man", "woman"))

# quick evaluation: do the neighbors share the context?
for w in ["graph", "court", "ticket"]:
    print(w, "->", [x for x, _ in wv.most_similar(w, topn=3)])
```

## 5. Topic models {#ch5}

A corpus of thousands of documents is too large to read, but it is usually about a few dozen themes. Topic models recover these themes without any labels: each topic is a probability distribution over words, and each document a mixture of topics.

::: thm
[Model 5.1 — LDA (Blei, Ng & Jordan, 2003): the full generative model]{.tag} For each document $d$ and each position $i$ of the corpus:
$$
\theta_d \sim \mathrm{Dir}(\alpha_{\mathrm{LDA}}),\quad z_{d,i}\mid\theta_d \sim \theta_d,\quad \varphi_k\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\beta_{\mathrm{LDA}}),\quad w_{d,i}\mid z_{d,i},\varphi \sim \varphi_{z_{d,i}}.
$$
A document is a mixture of $K$ topics; each word is drawn from the topic of its position. The hyperparameters carry the subscript LDA because $\alpha_t$ and $\beta_t$ denote the forward and backward variables of the HMM in ch. 6.

The likelihood $p(\mathbf{w})$ sums over all assignments $z$ — intractable ($K^{\#\mathrm{words}}$ terms): hence the *variational Bayes* inference (original paper) or *Gibbs sampling* (practical usage).

Connected reminders: EM from the ML module (variational inference is its Bayesian version); Markov chains ([Refresher Statistics](../m1p1-refresher-statistics/index.html#ch2) ch. 2, [Reinforcement Learning](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html#ch0) ch. 0 — the sampler is a chain whose stationary law is the posterior; geometric convergence under conditions).
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Collapsed Gibbs sampling: the update equation]{.tag} By integrating out $\theta,\varphi$ (Dirichlet–multinomial conjugacy), the law of an assignment $z_i$ given everything else depends only on *counts*:

::: key
[Key result — collapsed Gibbs update for LDA]{.tag}
$$
\mathbb{P}(z_i = k \mid z_{-i},\, w) \;\propto\; \underbrace{\frac{n_{k,w_i}^{-i}+\beta_{\mathrm{LDA}}}{n_k^{-i}+|\mathcal{V}|\beta_{\mathrm{LDA}}}}_{\text{does topic \(k\) like word \(w_i\)?}}\;\cdot\; \underbrace{\frac{n_{d,k}^{-i}+\alpha_{\mathrm{LDA}}}{n_d^{-i}+K\alpha_{\mathrm{LDA}}}}_{\text{does document \(d\) like topic \(k\)?}}
$$
:::

where $n_{k,w}$ = number of times topic $k$ has emitted $w$, $n_{d,k}$ = topic $k$ in $d$.

The exponent $-i$ means "without the current position".

Each $z_i$ is sampled sequentially, over thousands of passes; the topics emerge by reinforcement (the rich-get-richer property of Dirichlets).

::: proof
By conjugacy, the marginal of the corpus factorizes into multivariate beta functions:
$$
p(w,z\mid\alpha_{\mathrm{LDA}},\beta_{\mathrm{LDA}})=\prod_k \frac{B(n_{k,\cdot}+\beta_{\mathrm{LDA}})}{B(\beta_{\mathrm{LDA}})} \prod_d \frac{B(n_{d,\cdot}+\alpha_{\mathrm{LDA}})}{B(\alpha_{\mathrm{LDA}})}.
$$

The conditional $\mathbb{P}(z_i=k\mid\cdot)$ is the ratio $p(w,z_i=k,z_{-i})/p(z_{-i},w_{-i})$: all the factors not touching position $i$ cancel out, by a property of beta ratios:
$$
\frac{B(u+e_k)}{B(u)}=\frac{u_k}{\sum_j u_j} .
$$
This leaves the product of the two predictive factors above. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Choosing the hyperparameters and K]{.tag} Small $\alpha_{\mathrm{LDA}}$ = pure documents (few topics per document); small $\beta_{\mathrm{LDA}}$ = pure topics (distinctive words). The *asymmetric* version (a non-uniform vector $\alpha_{\mathrm{LDA}}$) lets a "noise" topic emerge. $K$ is chosen by validation (held-out perplexity) *or* by coherence — see below; the two criteria do not rank models in the same order, an important result of text mining.
:::

::: def
[Evaluation 5.3 — Perplexity vs coherence]{.tag} **Perplexity** (held-out):
$$
\mathrm{PPL}=\exp\big(-\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{test}}}\sum \log p(w_{\mathrm{test}})\big)
$$
with $p(w\mid d)=\sum_k \theta_{d,k}\varphi_{k,w}$ — but it correlates *poorly* with human judgment (Chang et al., 2009: models with lower perplexity may produce less interpretable topics).

**NPMI coherence**: for the $M$ most probable words of each topic, average
$$
\mathrm{NPMI}(u,v)=\frac{\log\dfrac{P(u,v)}{P(u)P(v)}}{-\log P(u,v)} \in [-1,1]
$$
over all pairs (probabilities estimated from document cooccurrences): it measures the actual collocation of the topic's words — well correlated with humans.

The engineer's rule: perplexity for predictive capacity, NPMI/$C_v$ for interpretability.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.4 — LSA: truncated SVD as the PCA of text]{.tag} On the TF-IDF matrix $\mathbf{X}$:
$$
\mathbf{X}\approx\mathbf{U}_k\Sigma_k\mathbf{V}_k^\top ;
$$
each *row* of $\mathbf{U}_k\Sigma_k$ gives one document's coordinates in the latent space (the rows of $\mathbf{X}$ are the documents). The $k$ dimensions are the directions of maximal *second moment* — not of variance, since $\mathbf{X}$ is not centered — and the coordinate columns are orthogonal, which makes them uncorrelated only after centering. The columns of $\mathbf{V}_k$ give the topics as signed word loadings (unlike LDA's distributions, they can be negative).

Key differences: LSA is linear, deterministic, fast; LDA is generative, models the counts, yields interpretable mixtures — but LSA captures *weighted cooccurrence* and is often sufficient for document similarity.

Link with PCA: PCA = SVD of the centered-scaled matrix (ML module); LSA = SVD of the TF-IDF matrix (no centering: the "mean" of text makes no sense).
:::

-   **After LDA**: BERTopic (embeddings + clustering + c-TF-IDF) for topics on contemporary corpora — consistent with the "embeddings, ch. 4" pipeline; for the industrial use of topics: monitoring, compliance, e-discovery, detection of emerging themes;
-   **Word Sense Induction**: applying clustering to *all the occurrences of a single word* (BERT contexts) reveals its senses — the joint Vazirgiannis–Buscaldi paper of ch. 9 does exactly that, with mutual information maximization;
-   **Topic models on graphs** (TopSBM, Gerlach et al., 2018): the idea extended to networks (see the Graph ML module).

## 6. Sequences and relations: NER, HMM, CRF, relation extraction {#ch6}

Some tasks need a label for every word rather than for the whole document: finding the names of persons and companies in a sentence, or the grammatical category of each word. Neighboring labels depend on each other (an entity that begins must continue), so this chapter uses models of the whole label sequence: hidden Markov models, then conditional random fields. It ends by linking the entities it finds into relations: the triples of a knowledge graph.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Sequence labeling]{.tag} Assign a label to each token: **POS** (grammatical category) or **NER** (named entities: PER, ORG, LOC…) in BIO ("**B**egin/**I**nside/**O**utside"): "*Kim*" = B-PER, "*Noel*" = I-PER. NER is the gateway to building knowledge graphs (entity + relation extraction, section 6.4).
:::

### 6.1. Hidden Markov models

:::: thm
[HMM: forward, backward, Viterbi — the recurrences derived]{.tag} HMM: hidden states $z_t$ (labels), emissions $\mathbb{P}(w_t\mid z_t)$, transitions $\mathbb{P}(z_t\mid z_{t-1})$. Notation: $\alpha_t(z)=\mathbb{P}(w_1,\dots,w_t,\,z_t=z)$ (**forward**) and $\beta_t(z)=\mathbb{P}(w_{t+1},\dots,w_T\mid z_t=z)$ (**backward**):
$$
\alpha_t(z)=\mathbb{P}(w_t\mid z)\sum_{z'}\alpha_{t-1}(z')\,\mathbb{P}(z\mid z'), \qquad \beta_t(z)=\sum_{z'}\mathbb{P}(z'\mid z)\,\mathbb{P}(w_{t+1}\mid z')\,\beta_{t+1}(z').
$$

::: proof
-   **Forward**: condition on $z_{t-1}$.
    $$
    \alpha_t(z)=\sum_{z'}\mathbb{P}(w_{1:t},z_{t-1}=z',z_t=z) =\sum_{z'}\underbrace{\mathbb{P}(w_{1:t-1},z_{t-1}=z')}_{\alpha_{t-1}(z')} \,\mathbb{P}(z\mid z')\,\mathbb{P}(w_t\mid z)
    $$
    — by the Markov property, given $z_{t-1}$ the pair $(z_t, w_t)$ does not depend on the earlier observations.
-   **Backward**: symmetric, conditioning on $z_{t+1}$.

Uses: likelihood $\mathbb{P}(w_{1:T})=\sum_z \alpha_T(z)$; marginal posteriors
$$
\mathbb{P}(z_t\mid w)=\alpha_t(z)\beta_t(z)/\mathbb{P}(w)
$$
— this is the E-step of an EM to train the HMM (ML module). All in $\mathcal{O}(T K^2)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Algorithm 6.2 — Viterbi: optimality by substructure]{.tag} The most likely label path satisfies the recursion
$$
\delta_t(z) = \max_{z'} \big[\delta_{t-1}(z')\, \mathbb{P}(z \mid z')\big]\ \mathbb{P}(w_t \mid z),\qquad \delta_1(z)=\mathbb{P}(z)\mathbb{P}(w_1\mid z),
$$
and the optimal labeling is read off by backtracking the argmaxes — $\mathcal{O}(T K^2)$ instead of $\mathcal{O}(K^T)$.

::: proof
Optimality: any optimal path arriving at $(t,z)$ has an optimal prefix up to $(t-1,z')$ — otherwise replacing the prefix with a better one increases the total probability (exchange argument: the future factors depend only on $z$, Markovian). So it suffices to follow the best predecessor: this is Bellman (RL module, ch. 2) on a Markov chain, with max instead of expectation. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Algorithm 6.3 — Baum–Welch: training an HMM without labels]{.tag} When only the words are observed (no tagged corpus), the initial law $\pi(z)=\mathbb{P}(z_1=z)$ and the tables $\mathbb{P}(z\mid z')$ and $\mathbb{P}(w\mid z)$ are learned by EM, with forward-backward as the E-step.

**E-step** — with the current parameters, compute $\alpha_t$, $\beta_t$ and the likelihood $\mathbb{P}(w_{1:T})$, then the posterior of each state and of each transition:
$$
\gamma_t(z)=\frac{\alpha_t(z)\,\beta_t(z)}{\mathbb{P}(w_{1:T})},
\qquad
\xi_t(z',z)=\frac{\alpha_{t-1}(z')\,\mathbb{P}(z\mid z')\,\mathbb{P}(w_t\mid z)\,\beta_t(z)}{\mathbb{P}(w_{1:T})}.
$$

**M-step** — re-estimate each table by its *expected* relative counts:
$$
\hat\pi(z)=\gamma_1(z),
\qquad
\hat{\mathbb{P}}(z\mid z')=\frac{\sum_{t=2}^{T}\xi_t(z',z)}{\sum_{t=2}^{T}\gamma_{t-1}(z')},
\qquad
\hat{\mathbb{P}}(w\mid z)=\frac{\sum_{t}\gamma_t(z)\,\mathbf{1}[w_t=w]}{\sum_{t}\gamma_t(z)}.
$$
With several sentences, the numerators and the denominators are summed over the sentences.

::: proof
The M-step is the maximum-likelihood estimate of a *tagged* corpus — relative counts, as for Naive Bayes in Theorem 3.1 — with each hard count $\mathbf{1}[z_t=z]$ replaced by its posterior expectation $\gamma_t(z)$, and each transition count by $\xi_t(z',z)$.

This is the EM recipe of the ML module: maximize the expected complete-data log-likelihood under the posterior of the hidden states. EM never decreases $\mathbb{P}(w_{1:T})$, but it reaches only a local maximum, so initialize from a small tagged corpus when one exists. Each iteration costs $\mathcal{O}(TK^2)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

In practice, compute in log space or rescale $\alpha_t$ at each step: the probabilities underflow after a few hundred words. The [Speech Technology](../m2-speech-technology/index.html#ch1) module writes $o_t$ for the observations, $A$ for the transition matrix and $b_j(o)$ for the emissions; the recursions are the same.
::::

```python
# Toy Viterbi: 2-state POS tagging (N noun, V verb), 4-word vocabulary
import numpy as np
W = ["le", "chat", "mange", "souris"]
p_z0  = np.array([.9, .1])                      # P(z1)
A     = np.array([[.8,.2],[.3,.7]])             # P(z_t | z_{t-1})  rows=prev
B     = np.array([[.6,.3,.02,.08],
                  [.0,.02,.9,.08]])             # P(w | z)  columns=words
seq   = [0,1,2,3]                               # "le chat mange souris"

delta = B[:, seq[0]] * p_z0                     # initialization
back  = []
for w in seq[1:]:
    m = delta[:, None] * A * B[:, w][None, :]   # (prev, cur)
    back.append(m.argmax(0)); delta = m.max(0)
z = [delta.argmax()]
for bp in reversed(back): z.append(bp[z[-1]])
print("labels:", [["N","V"][i] for i in reversed(z)])
```

### 6.2. Conditional random fields

::: thm
[CRF (Lafferty et al., 2001): the discriminative approach]{.tag} An HMM models $\mathbb{P}(w,z)$ *jointly* (generative); a CRF models $\mathbb{P}(z\mid w)$ directly:
$$
\mathbb{P}(z\mid w)=\frac{\exp\big(\sum_{t}\theta^\top f(z_{t-1},z_t,w,t)\big)}{Z(w)}, \qquad \nabla_\theta \log\mathbb{P}(z^\star\mid w) = F(z^\star, w)-\mathbb{E}_{p(z\mid w)}\big[F(z, w)\big]
$$
(with $z^\star$ the gold labeling and $F(z, w) = \sum_t f(z_{t-1}, z_t, w, t)$ the summed features) — *arbitrary* features over the whole sequence: word identity, suffixes, capitalization, shape of the neighbor, hyphen, position…, plus transition features $z_{t-1}\to z_t$ (whose learned weights make O→I-PER very unlikely: an entity start must be B).

**Computing $\log Z(w)$: the forward algorithm.** The partition function sums over the $K^T$ labelings, but it factorizes along the chain. Write the potential of one transition, with a start state $z_0$ before $t=1$, as
$$
\psi_t(z',z)=\exp\big(\theta^\top f(z',z,w,t)\big).
$$
Then
$$
\alpha_1(z)=\psi_1(z_0,z),\qquad \alpha_t(z)=\sum_{z'}\alpha_{t-1}(z')\,\psi_t(z',z),\qquad Z(w)=\sum_{z}\alpha_T(z),
$$
the HMM forward recursion with potentials in place of probabilities, in $\mathcal{O}(TK^2)$. In practice it runs in log space, which avoids overflow:
$$
\log\alpha_t(z)=\operatorname{logsumexp}_{z'}\big[\log\alpha_{t-1}(z')+\theta^\top f(z',z,w,t)\big].
$$

A backward pass $\beta_t$, defined in the same way from $t=T$ down, gives the pairwise marginals
$$
\mathbb{P}(z_{t-1}=z',\,z_t=z\mid w)=\frac{\alpha_{t-1}(z')\,\psi_t(z',z)\,\beta_t(z)}{Z(w)},
$$
from which the expectation $\mathbb{E}_{p(z\mid w)}[F(z,w)]$ in the gradient is a sum over $t$, $z'$ and $z$. Viterbi with the same potentials gives the best labeling.

The gain over HMM: no "waste" in modeling the words, rich features, arbitrary interactions — long the state of the art for NER (CoNLL-2003).
:::

### 6.3. Decoding and evaluating entities

::: def
[BIO decoding and entity-level NER evaluation]{.tag} Per-token predictions must be converted into *spans*: an entity = a B-X (I-X)\* sequence. **Entity** evaluation (not token): an entity is correct iff both type *and* exact boundaries match;
$$
\mathrm{P}=\frac{\#\text{correct}}{\#\text{predicted}},\qquad \mathrm{R}=\frac{\#\text{correct}}{\#\text{gold}},\qquad F_1=\frac{2PR}{P+R}.
$$

Token-level F1 (lenient about boundaries) usually overestimates entity-level F1, but not always. If the gold has a 10-token entity and a 1-token entity and the system finds only the short one, entity-level F1 is 0.67 while token-level F1 is 0.17. Always report entity-level F1 (the conlleval standard).

Industrial reflex: audit *boundary* errors ("Banque de France" truncated) separately from *type* errors (PER vs ORG).
:::

::: note
[Today]{.tag} Transformers label token by token (per-token softmax + BIO decoding; the head is often a *linear-chain CRF* or a simple softmax with BIO constraints in post-processing); the `spaCy` and `transformers` libraries (the `ner` pipeline) deliver the state of the art in a few lines. The lab of section 6.4 turns the tagged entities into relations that feed the GraphRAG lab of the Graph ML module (ch. 10); ch. 8 of this course assembles the full pipeline.
:::

### 6.4. Relation extraction {#relation-extraction}

NER finds the entities of a text; relation extraction decides which relation, if any, links two of them. The output is a set of triples (head, relation, tail): the edges of a knowledge graph, which the GraphRAG of the [Graph ML](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch10) module (ch. 10) then searches.

::: def
[Definition 6.4 — Relation extraction]{.tag} Given a passage and two entity mentions $e_1, e_2$ found by NER, predict a relation $r \in \mathcal{R}\cup\{\text{none}\}$ from a fixed inventory $\mathcal{R}$ (place of birth, director, employer…).

Each positive decision yields a directed *triple* $(e_1, r, e_2)$ — head, relation, tail — stored with its source passage. The triples $(e_1, r, e_2)$ and $(e_2, r, e_1)$ are different.

*Example*: "Marie Curie was born in Warsaw" gives (Marie Curie, place of birth, Warsaw).
:::

-   **Pipeline vs joint.** A *pipeline* runs NER, then classifies every ordered pair of mentions of a sentence ($m(m-1)$ candidates for $m$ mentions). It is modular and easy to debug, but NER errors propagate: a missed entity is a missed triple.

    A *joint* model predicts entities and relations together — by table filling, or by a sequence-to-sequence model that generates the linearized triples (REBEL, Huguet Cabot & Navigli, 2021). It removes the propagation but is harder to train and to audit.
-   **Entity markers on an encoder** (Baldini Soares et al., 2019; Zhong & Chen, 2021). Wrap the two mentions in marker tokens, "[E1] Marie Curie [/E1] was born in [E2] Warsaw [/E2]", encode the sentence with a BERT-type model (ch. 7), concatenate the output vectors at the two opening markers and classify:
    $$
    p(r\mid s,e_1,e_2)=\mathrm{softmax}\big(W\,[h_{[E1]};\,h_{[E2]}]+b\big).
    $$
    Typed markers such as [E1:PER] add the NER type for free. Training follows the fine-tuning Protocol 7.1.
-   **Distant supervision** (Mintz et al., 2009): labels without annotators. Align a knowledge base such as Wikidata with the text, and label every sentence that mentions both entities of a known triple with that relation.

    The labels are noisy in both directions: "Obama visited Hawaii" is labeled *place of birth* (a false positive), and true facts missing from the base become false negatives. Multi-instance learning (Riedel et al., 2010) only assumes that *at least one* sentence of each bag expresses the relation. A small hand-checked test set remains necessary.
-   **Few-shot LLM extraction with a JSON schema.** Prompt an instruction-tuned LLM with the relation inventory, two to five annotated examples and the passage (the mechanism of the few-shot box in section 7.2), and require an answer that validates against a schema:

    ```json
    {"type": "object", "required": ["triples"],
     "properties": {"triples": {"type": "array", "items": {
       "type": "object", "required": ["head", "relation", "tail", "evidence"],
       "properties": {"head": {"type": "string"}, "tail": {"type": "string"},
                      "relation": {"enum": ["place of birth", "director", "employer"]},
                      "evidence": {"type": "string"}}}}}}
    ```

    Validate every answer (re-ask on invalid JSON or an unknown relation) and drop the triples whose head or tail does not occur in the passage, a cheap guard against invented entities. No training data is needed, but every passage costs tokens; on a fixed schema with a few thousand labeled examples, a fine-tuned extractor is usually more accurate and far cheaper.

::: def
[Definition 6.5 — Triple evaluation: strict and relaxed micro-F1]{.tag} Pool the predicted and the gold triples of all documents (micro-averaging), then
$$
\mathrm{P}=\frac{\#\text{correct}}{\#\text{predicted}},\qquad \mathrm{R}=\frac{\#\text{correct}}{\#\text{gold}},\qquad F_1=\frac{2PR}{P+R}.
$$

Under the **strict** criterion, a predicted triple is correct when its head, relation and tail all match a gold triple after light normalization (case, spaces, punctuation).

Under the **relaxed** criterion, the relation must match, and the head and the tail need only refer to the same entity: the same knowledge-base identifier after entity resolution, or one string contained in the other ("Curie" for "Marie Curie").

The gap between the two scores measures boundary and alias errors, as the token/entity gap does for NER.
:::

::: ex
[Example 6.6 — Scoring an extractor]{.tag} A passage has 4 gold triples. The extractor outputs 5: 2 match exactly, and 1 more matches after alias resolution ("M. Curie").

-   Strict: $P=2/5=0.4$, $R=2/4=0.5$, $F_1\approx 0.444$.
-   Relaxed: $P=3/5=0.6$, $R=3/4=0.75$, $F_1\approx 0.667$.

The extractor finds the right facts more often than its strict score says: the next fix is entity resolution, not the relation classifier.
:::

::: ex
[Lab sheet — session 8: from tagged entities to triples]{.tag}

1.  **NER.** Train a CRF with hand-crafted features (`sklearn-crfsuite`) and run a pretrained transformer tagger on CoNLL-2003 (Tjong Kim Sang & De Meulder, 2003). Report entity-level F1 with `seqeval`, and sort 20 errors into boundary and type errors.
2.  **Relations.** Take 200 development questions of 2WikiMultiHopQA (Ho et al., COLING 2020): each comes with its supporting Wikipedia paragraphs and gold *evidence triples*. Run the few-shot JSON extractor on the supporting paragraphs, restricted to the relations that occur in the evidences.
3.  **Score.** Report strict and relaxed triple micro-F1 against the evidence triples (Definition 6.5), and read 10 false positives.
4.  **Export.** Write the triples to a CSV file (head, relation, tail, source paragraph). It is the input of the GraphRAG lab of [Graph ML](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch10) (ch. 10); Exercise 12 adds a supervised extractor to this sheet.
:::

## 7. Transformers for NLP {#ch7}

The models of the previous chapters give each word one vector whatever its context, and read a sentence through a short window at best. Transformers compute for each token a representation that depends on the whole sentence; pretrained once on a large corpus, they are then adapted to each task with little labeled data. This chapter states the architecture in one page, then applies it to text: pretrained families, fine-tuning, sentence embeddings and a first retrieval-augmented generator.

### 7.1. The transformer block in one page {#transformer-block}

::: def
[The transformer block, self-contained]{.tag} **Input.** A sentence of $n$ tokens becomes a matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$, one row per token: the token's embedding (a row of a learned table with $|\mathcal{V}|$ rows) plus a *position* vector. Positions are learned vectors (BERT) or fixed sinusoids,
$$
P_{t,2i}=\sin\big(t/10000^{2i/d}\big),\qquad P_{t,2i+1}=\cos\big(t/10000^{2i/d}\big).
$$
Without them, self-attention is permutation-equivariant: the sentence would be read as a bag of words again (ch. 2). Recent LLMs rotate queries and keys instead (RoPE).

**One attention head.** With $W_Q, W_K, W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d_k}$,
$$
Q=XW_Q,\quad K=XW_K,\quad V=XW_V,\qquad \mathrm{Attn}(X)=\mathrm{softmax}\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M\Big)V,
$$
with the softmax taken row by row. Row $i$ of the output is a weighted average of the value vectors, weighted by how well query $i$ matches each key. The scale $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps the logits of order one: if the entries of a query and a key are independent, with mean zero and variance one, their dot product has variance $d_k$.

**Mask.** With $M=0$ every token sees the whole sentence (encoder, BERT). The *causal* mask, $M_{ij}=-\infty$ for $j>i$ and $0$ otherwise, lets token $i$ see only the past (decoder, GPT), so the model learns to predict every next token of a sentence in one pass.

**Multi-head.** $h$ heads with $d_k = d/h$ run in parallel; their outputs are concatenated and mixed by $W_O\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$:
$$
\mathrm{MHA}(X)=\big[\mathrm{head}_1,\dots,\mathrm{head}_h\big]\,W_O .
$$
Each head can follow a different relation (syntax, coreference, position).

**Block.** Each of the $L$ blocks adds two sublayers to a *residual stream*, with a LayerNorm before each (pre-LN, the modern choice; BERT and the original transformer normalize after the sum):
$$
H=X+\mathrm{MHA}\big(\mathrm{LN}(X)\big),\qquad Y=H+\mathrm{FFN}\big(\mathrm{LN}(H)\big).
$$
The feed-forward network acts on each token separately, $\mathrm{FFN}(x)=W_2\,\mathrm{GELU}(W_1x+b_1)+b_2$, with a hidden width of about $4d$. The residual sums let the gradient cross dozens of blocks.

**Families and cost.** Encoder only (BERT, no mask) for understanding tasks; decoder only (GPT, causal mask) for generation; encoder–decoder (T5), where the decoder's queries also attend to the encoder's outputs (cross-attention). Attention costs $\mathcal{O}(n^2 d)$ per layer and the FFN $\mathcal{O}(n d^2)$: long inputs are expensive, which is one reason why RAG (section 7.4) sends only a few retrieved passages to the model.

**Going deeper.** Proofs and a PyTorch block: [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch6), ch. 6. The same block from the systems side: [Deep Learning (P2)](../m1p2-deep-learning-p2/index.html#ch0), ch. 0. Modern variants (RoPE, GQA, MoE): [M2 LLMs](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch2), ch. 2.
:::

### 7.2. Pretrained families: BERT, GPT, T5 {#pretrained-families}

::: thm
[BERT (Devlin et al., 2019): MLM + NSP in detail]{.tag} Bidirectional encoder, pretrained on two tasks.

1.  **Masked LM**: 15 % of tokens drawn; among them 80 % replaced by `[MASK]`, 10 % by a random word, 10 % unchanged; the original token is predicted (output: per-position classification). The mixing avoids a pretraining/fine-tuning mismatch (the model will never see `[MASK]` downstream again) and forces a robust representation.
2.  **Next Sentence Prediction**: classify whether two sentences follow each other (the pair `[CLS]` A `[SEP]` B) — a weak task, abandoned by RoBERTa in favor of more data.

Result: `[CLS]` = sentence representation; one model, dozens of tasks via a simple head layer.
:::

::: thm
[GPT (Radford et al.) and T5 (Raffel et al., 2019)]{.tag} **GPT**: causal decoder — $\mathcal{L}=-\sum_t\log p(x_t\mid x_{<t})$, pretraining = predicting the next token; generative by construction, zero task-specific architecture (this is the family extended in M2).

**T5**: everything in text-to-text — span corruption (masking continuous fragments and regenerating them), every task (classification, translation, QA…) formulated as textual input→output; it unifies MLM and CLM.
:::

::: note
[Zero- and few-shot classification with a causal LM]{.tag} A decoder can classify text without any gradient step.

1.  Write a prompt: an instruction, $k$ labeled examples ("Review: … Sentiment: positive"), then the test input followed by "Sentiment:". With $k=0$ it is zero-shot.
2.  Score each label by the model's probability of the label's tokens after the prompt, and take the argmax — or let the model generate and parse its answer.
3.  Accuracy moves by several points with the choice and the *order* of the examples and with the label words. Dividing each label's probability by its probability after a content-free input such as "N/A" removes part of this bias (Zhao et al., 2021).
4.  Compare with fine-tuning (Protocol 7.1) on the same test split before choosing (ch. 3).
5.  [M2 LLMs](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch4) (ch. 4.0) studies in-context learning in depth; [Graph ML](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch10) (ch. 10.2) applies the same mechanism to graphs written as text.
:::

### 7.3. Fine-tuning and sentence embeddings {#fine-tuning}

::: def
[Protocol 7.1 — Full fine-tuning (the stable recipe)]{.tag}

1.  **Head**: a linear layer $\mathrm{Linear}(d, K)$ on `[CLS]` (classification) or per position (NER, POS);
2.  **Optimizer**: AdamW, learning rate $\{2\times10^{-5}, 3\times10^{-5}, 5\times10^{-5}\}$ — a short grid, fine-tuning is sensitive but flat around the optimum; linear warmup for 10 % then linear decay;
3.  **Epochs**: 2 to 4 (beyond that: brutal overfitting on small corpora — watch the dev set); batch 16-32;
4.  **Small corpora (<1k)**: freeze the lower layers, layer-wise decay (*layer-wise lr decay*), or adapters/LoRA (added parameters << 1 %; the mathematics in [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch7) 7.3, the LLM practice in [M2 LLMs](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch4) 4.3);
5.  **Cost**: distillation (DistilBERT: 40 % fewer parameters, 60 % faster at inference, \~97 % of the performance of BERT), int8 quantization — the performance/cost trade-off is an engineering criterion, deepened in M2 (LLMs 4.3 for distillation and 6.4 for quantization; ML Ops).
:::

::: ex
[Lab sheet — session 9: fine-tuning a small encoder by hand]{.tag} The loop below implements Protocol 7.1 without the `Trainer` class, so that every step is visible: tokenization, padding per batch, AdamW with 10 % warmup and linear decay, gradient clipping, evaluation on the dev set after each epoch, and keeping the best epoch. It fine-tunes DistilBERT (66M parameters) on SST-2 (binary sentiment) on a free GPU tier.

1.  Run it, and plot the dev macro-F1 per epoch for two learning rates of the protocol's grid.
2.  Swap in a French encoder and dataset (CamemBERT on the Allociné reviews, for instance) and change nothing else.
3.  Exercise 10 then compares this model with the TF-IDF baselines of ch. 3 as the training set grows.
:::

```python
import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import (AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification,
                          DataCollatorWithPadding, get_linear_schedule_with_warmup)
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score

name = "distilbert-base-uncased"                         # small encoder, 66M parameters
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
ds = load_dataset("nyu-mll/glue", "sst2")                # columns: sentence, label, idx
ds = ds.map(lambda b: tok(b["sentence"], truncation=True, max_length=128),
            batched=True, remove_columns=["sentence", "idx"])
collate = DataCollatorWithPadding(tok)                   # pads per batch, renames label -> labels
train = DataLoader(ds["train"], batch_size=32, shuffle=True, collate_fn=collate)
dev = DataLoader(ds["validation"], batch_size=64, collate_fn=collate)

torch.manual_seed(0)
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(name, num_labels=2).to(device)
epochs = 3
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=2e-5, weight_decay=0.01)
steps = epochs * len(train)
sched = get_linear_schedule_with_warmup(opt, int(0.1 * steps), steps)  # 10 % warmup, linear decay

def evaluate():
    model.eval(); ys, ps = [], []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for b in dev:
            b = {k: v.to(device) for k, v in b.items()}
            ps += model(**b).logits.argmax(-1).tolist(); ys += b["labels"].tolist()
    model.train()
    return f1_score(ys, ps, average="macro")

best = 0.0
for epoch in range(epochs):
    for b in train:
        b = {k: v.to(device) for k, v in b.items()}
        loss = model(**b).loss                           # cross-entropy of the head on [CLS]
        loss.backward()
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        opt.step(); sched.step(); opt.zero_grad()
    f1 = evaluate()
    print(f"epoch {epoch}: dev macro-F1 {f1:.3f}")
    if f1 > best:                                        # keep the best epoch only
        best = f1; model.save_pretrained("best"); tok.save_pretrained("best")
```

:::: thm
[Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019): siamese training objectives]{.tag} To encode sentences in a comparable space (search, clustering, RAG), two copies of BERT with shared weights encode the two sentences of a pair, and mean pooling of the output vectors gives $u$ and $v$. The paper uses the objective that fits the data at hand:

-   **classification** on NLI pairs (SNLI and MultiNLI: entailment, contradiction, neutral), for its main models, with a cross-entropy on
    $$
    \hat y=\mathrm{softmax}\big(W_t\,[u;\,v;\,|u-v|]\big);
    $$
-   **regression** on STS pairs: the cosine of $u$ and $v$ is fitted to the gold similarity score with a squared loss;
-   **triplet**, for its Wikipedia-sections data: with an anchor $a$, a positive $p$ and a negative $n$,
    $$
    \mathcal{L}=\max\big(0,\ d(a,p)-d(a,n)+\varepsilon\big).
    $$

::: proof
Triplet loss. If the margin is respected ($d(a,p)+\varepsilon\le d(a,n)$), the loss is zero: nothing to learn. Otherwise, the gradient $\nabla = \nabla d(a,p)-\nabla d(a,n)$ *pulls* the anchor toward the positive and *pushes* it away from the negative; with this hinge loss, the size of the update does not depend on how much the margin is violated. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Later sentence-transformers models are mostly trained on (query, positive) pairs with the *multiple negatives ranking loss* (Henderson et al., 2017). In a batch of $B$ pairs $(a_i, p_i)$, the other positives $p_j$, $j\ne i$, serve as negatives:
$$
\mathcal{L}=-\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^{B}\log\frac{\exp\big(\cos(a_i,p_i)/\tau\big)}{\sum_{j=1}^{B}\exp\big(\cos(a_i,p_j)/\tau\big)},
$$
with a temperature $\tau$ of about $0.05$. These in-batch negatives are mostly random, hence easy. *Hard* negatives — passages that BM25 ranks high but that are not relevant — are mined and added explicitly, and they are what sharpens the space. Such embeddings index the corpora of RAG systems (section 7.4; M2 LLMs ch. 7 for dense retrieval and reranking).
::::

::: note
[French: CamemBERT, FlauBERT, JuriBERT]{.tag} CamemBERT (Martin et al., 2020): RoBERTa retrained on 138 GB of French text — the reference French model; FlauBERT: an academic French BERT; **JuriBERT** (Douka et al., 2021 — research from this course, ch. 9): an adaptation to *legal* French, where the vocabulary (doctrine, grievances, appeal) confuses general models. Multilingual: mBERT, XLM-R (100+ languages, shared embeddings — at the price of capacity diluted per language).
:::

```python
from transformers import pipeline

classifier = pipeline("text-classification",
                      model="distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english")
print(classifier("Graph RAG is a game changer for enterprise search."))

ner = pipeline("ner", aggregation_strategy="simple")
print(ner("Michalis Vazirgiannis teaches at Ecole Polytechnique."))

# sentence embeddings for RAG (cf. section 7.4 and M2 LLMs ch. 7)
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
enc = SentenceTransformer("paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2")
print(enc.encode(["résumé automatique", "automatic summarization"]).shape)
```

### 7.4. A minimal RAG pipeline {#minimal-rag}

A language model answers from what it memorized during pretraining: it does not know a company's documents, and it can state wrong facts fluently. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG; Lewis et al., 2020) first retrieves passages from a corpus, then asks the model to answer from them. This section builds the minimal version from pieces of this course: BM25 (ch. 2), Sentence-BERT (7.3) and the ranking metrics of section 2.1.

[M2 LLMs](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch7) (ch. 7) goes in depth (reranking, evaluation at scale). The GraphRAG of [Graph ML](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch10) (ch. 10) and the LLM agents of [Reinforcement Learning](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html#ch7) (ch. 7) start from this pipeline.

::: def
[Definition 7.2 — Retrieve-then-read]{.tag}

1.  **Chunking.** Split each document into passages of about 100 to 300 words, overlapping by 10 to 20 % so that a sentence cut at a boundary survives whole in one chunk. Keep the document and the position of each chunk, for citations. Paragraphs or sections, when the documents have them, beat fixed windows.
2.  **Indexing.** Index the chunks twice: an inverted index scored by BM25 (Definition 2.6, Model 2.4), and a matrix of normalized Sentence-BERT vectors, in which the cosine is a dot product.
3.  **Retrieval.** For a query, take the top $k$ chunks of each retriever ($k$ from 3 to 10). *Hybrid* search fuses the two rankings by reciprocal rank fusion (Cormack et al., 2009), which needs no calibration between the two kinds of score:
    $$
    \mathrm{RRF}(c)=\sum_{r\,\in\,\{\text{sparse},\ \text{dense}\}}\frac{1}{60+\mathrm{rank}_r(c)},
    $$
    where a chunk absent from a ranking gets no term from it.
4.  **Reading.** Put the $k$ chunks, numbered, into a prompt that asks for an answer *from these passages only*, with citations [n], and for "not in the passages" when they do not contain it.
:::

-   **Sparse or dense?** BM25 wins on rare exact strings — product codes, names, article numbers, the tickets of 8.4 — that a sentence encoder blurs. Dense retrieval wins on paraphrases and synonyms ("car" for "automobile", ch. 4), and across languages with a multilingual encoder. Hybrid fusion is the safe default; measure before choosing.
-   **How many chunks?** A larger $k$ raises recall but lengthens the prompt (cost, latency), and models use the middle of a long context less well than its ends.

::: def
[Evaluation 7.3 — Retrieval recall and faithfulness]{.tag} Evaluate the two stages separately.

-   **Retrieval**: on questions whose supporting passages are known, Recall@k (Definition 2.7) is the share of the supporting chunks found in the top $k$, and MRR scores the first one. A passage that is not retrieved cannot be used by any generator.
-   **Answer**: exact match or token F1 against a reference answer, when one exists.
-   **Faithfulness spot-check**: on a sample of 20 to 50 answers, check by hand that each claim is supported by a cited chunk. Report the share of supported claims and the share of answers that cite nothing. An answer can be right but unsupported (memorized), or supported but wrong (a misleading chunk).
:::

::: ex
[Example 7.4 — Recall@5 before and after fusion]{.tag} A two-hop question ("Where was the director of *The Last Emperor* born?") has two supporting chunks: $s_1$ about the film, $s_2$ about its director.

-   BM25 returns $(s_1, a, b, c, d)$: Recall@5 is $1/2$.
-   The dense retriever returns $(e, s_2, f, a, g)$, with $s_1$ only at rank 7: Recall@5 is $1/2$.
-   Fuse the top 7 of each list, in which only $a$ and $s_1$ appear twice. The four best RRF scores are
    $$
